claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory calculations can be used to predict ferromagnetic ground states in complex alloy systems.
Relevant magnetic configurations can be assessed by comparing the total energies of ferromagnetic, non-spin-polarized, and antiferromagnetic calculations.
The proposed calculations represent zero-temperature equilibrium conditions under periodic boundary conditions.
Localized magnetic moments on constituent atoms give rise to exchange splitting and associated electronic-band-structure changes.
Including spin polarization in DFT permits evaluation of energy stabilization associated with exchange interactions.
A ferromagnetic configuration with a lower total energy than the tested non-magnetic or antiferromagnetic configurations indicates a ferromagnetic ground state within the calculation.
The candidate alloy's ferromagnetic state will have a lower calculated total energy than the baseline state.
DFT-based magnetic-ground-state predictions are most reliable when the employed approximations adequately capture electron-correlation effects.
Strong electron correlations can reduce the accuracy of DFT predictions of magnetic ground states.
Significant finite-temperature effects can reduce the accuracy of a zero-temperature DFT prediction.
Fluctuations at elevated temperatures can introduce uncertainty into magnetic-ordering predictions based on zero-temperature energy differences.
Low-temperature SQUID magnetometry or neutron diffraction can be used to experimentally assess the magnetic ground state.
Magnetic hysteresis and a measurable Curie temperature are proposed as evidence of ferromagnetic order.
